title: How To Handle Temper Tantrums, Emotional Outbursts, And Other Outrageously Immature Behavior
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses how teachers should respond when a student has an emotional meltdown or tantrum in class, behavior he notes is becoming more common even among older elementary and middle school students. He lays out a seven-step protocol: protect the rest of the class by having them steer clear, wait without intervening, observe silently until the student calms down, resume the lesson as if nothing happened, stay away from the student for a couple of hours, escalate straight to a stronger consequence like an extended time-out for dangerous behavior, and inform parents with facts only. He pushes back on the common advice to talk the incident through with the student afterward, arguing that doing so tends to excuse the behavior rather than build accountability. The article concludes that consistent accountability, not conversation, is what actually teaches emotional control.
points: Immediately shift focus to protecting the rest of the class rather than engaging the upset student.
Wait and silently observe instead of rushing in to calm the student down.
Resume the lesson as normal once things settle, without lecturing or dwelling on the incident.
For dangerous outbursts, skip the warning/time-out sequence and go straight to an extended consequence.
Avoid "talking it out" afterward - hold the student accountable instead of excusing the behavior.
quotes: Pouting and stewing over the “unfairness,” the student loses the inner battle for control and loosens a torrent of outrage, tumbling from the mouth and quaking through the body.
So as soon as you notice a student losing control, shift your focus to the rest of your class. Ask them to stay clear of the ill-tempered student.
Continue waiting while keeping an eye on both the student in question and the rest of your class. Don’t say anything to the student.
For potentially dangerous situations, you reserve the right to jump past the warning and time-out steps and go directly to an extended time-out. A half day is reasonable.
Too often, though, talking it out has the effect of absolving the student of responsibility. It gives credence to the perceived injustice.
Most children who lose emotional control have been subject to too much talk. And not enough action.
